NEPA Decarbonization Technology Analysis: Deliverable 2

Determinations of Significance Across Resource Areas

Published

July 9, 2026

Draft status

This report reflects the validated extraction; see Methods & required caveats for the applicable limitations.

This report delivers:

Determinations of significance across resource areas; factors that contribute to a determination of “significant impact,” starting with mitigated FONSIs.

Context

When a clean-energy project — a solar farm, a transmission line — needs federal approval, the lead agency (here, BLM or the Department of Energy) studies its environmental impact and makes a judgment call: is the impact “significant” or not?

That one word decides a lot. If the agency finds the impact not significant, the project moves ahead on a faster track (a document called a Finding of No Significant Impact, or FONSI). If it finds the impact significant, that triggers a much longer, more demanding review.

Often the agency lands in between: “this impact would be significant — unless the developer commits to specific measures to reduce it.” That is a mitigated finding, and it is the most revealing case, because it shows the exact line the agency drew and what it required to stay on the safe side of it.

So this deliverable answers: across these clean-energy projects, how do agencies decide what counts as “significant” in each environmental area (air, water, wildlife, cultural sites, and so on) — and what mitigation do they demand to avoid that label? Answering it means reading and coding a judgment call out of thousands of dense decision documents — far more than anyone could review by hand. The workflow below is how we do that reliably.

Workflow

The approach pairs the scale of automation with the reliability of human judgment: software and AI do the reading at a scale no person could, while analysts define the scope, hold the checkpoints, and grade the AI against their own answer key before any result counts.

1 · Scope
Clean-energy FONSIs led by BLM or the DOE family — 258 documents across 193 projects, each dated to its regulatory era
↓
2 · Gather documents
Pull the FONSI and supporting EA documents from the NEPATEC 2.0 corpus, then use text-pattern (regex) rules to locate the specific sections where significance findings live
↓
3 · Extract the judgment calls
Automated: the flagged passages go to Claude (Sonnet 5), which codes each one — outcome, resource area, threshold, mitigation.
In parallel — the answer key: two analysts independently hand-label a 400-passage sample and an adjudicator settles their disagreements
↓
4 · Validate
Score the AI against the held-out human labels (class agreement 0.81) before any result counts
↓
5 · Analyze and report
Validated findings become this report and a source-linked data table — every number traces to its page
The five steps of the analysis — each card matches a numbered step below.

Why the results are trustworthy: every determination is traceable to the exact document, page, and passage; the AI is scored against human labels before it is used; and the project set is scoped so comparisons are fair.

What the two document types tell us

A significance call can land on either side of the line, and the two document types record opposite outcomes — so we analyze them separately rather than pooling them:

  • FONSIs are the below-the-line record. The agency concluded the impact is not significant. This is where the mitigated cases live — impacts that would have been significant without committed measures. FONSIs tell us how agencies stay under the line, and what they require to get there.
  • EISs are the above-the-line record. These are impacts the agency judged significant (and, at the extreme, significant and unavoidable). They tell us which resources actually cross the line.

This report presents the FONSI analysis, which is complete and validated. The EIS analysis runs the same machinery on a separate corpus; its answer key is already built and it awaits its extraction pass (see Scope decisions).

Figure 1 sets the scale: the clean-energy universe splits into a larger EIS corpus and a smaller FONSI corpus, and within the FONSIs the analysis touches every major resource area.

Because a FONSI is by definition a not-significant finding, a “significant” determination inside one is an anomaly — a would-be-significant-absent-mitigation phrasing, a rejected alternative, or a mis-read. Such cases are a fraction of a percent here and are flagged for review, not reported as findings. The significant side of the story is the EIS analysis.

FONSI analysis

Across 193 clean-energy projects (BLM + DOE family), the FONSI corpus yields 1,990 distinct significance determinations — one per document × resource area × outcome — drawn from 258 decision documents.

Key takeaways (FONSI track)
  • Most clean-energy FONSIs are mitigated. About 58% of these documents reach “no significant impact” only because the developer commits to specific measures — the impact would have been significant otherwise.
  • A handful of resources carry the mitigation. Biological resources, soils/geology, water, and cultural/historic sites are where projects most often sit at the line and are pulled under it — biological alone is mitigation-dependent in ~30% of its determinations.
  • The below-the-line default is “no significant impact.” Across resource areas, outright no-significant-impact is the most common outcome; genuinely significant findings live in the EIS record, not here.
  • The numbers are validated. The extraction agrees with a hand-labeled human answer key at 0.81 on the significance class (held-out test) before any figure in this report was produced.

How accurate is the extraction?

Every determination is machine-extracted, so before any number is reported the pipeline is scored against a hand-labeled answer key: two independent reviewers coded a stratified 400-window sample, a third adjudicated their disagreements, and 30% was held out as an untouched test. The held-out column is the honest score.

Table 1: Extraction accuracy versus the hand-labeled gold set, full sample and held-out test.
What the pipeline is scored on All 400 Held-out test
Finds a determination (per passage) 0.97 0.98
Assigns the right resource 0.88 0.89
Gets the significance class right 0.78 0.81
Flags mitigation-dependence 0.61 0.62
Identifies the regulatory threshold 0.71 0.66
Scores are F1 (0–1), except the threshold row, which is accuracy. Held-out = the 30% of the gold set the pipeline never influenced.

In plain terms: the extraction almost never misses a determination and places it in the right resource area ~89% of the time; it agrees with the human coders on the significance class at 0.81 — the standard bar for this kind of task. The one weaker signal is mitigation-dependence, discussed at the end of this section.

Why the last two scores are lower — and why it doesn’t undercut the findings. Both are secondary attributes, not the core call, and both are genuinely harder:

  • Mitigation-dependence (0.62). Deciding whether a conclusion depends on committed mitigation is one of the hardest judgments in the whole task — our two human coders themselves agreed only ~68% of the time on the fine line between “less than significant” and “less than significant with mitigation.” On top of that, the pipeline’s structured mitigation flag is tagged at the document level, so it over-attributes across a multi-resource passage, and its precision is ultimately bounded by upstream tagging. We handle this by reporting mitigation at the document level (where it is robust) and using the precise per-resource signal for the resource-level breakdown — so the numbers you see below are the high-precision measure, not the noisy flag.
  • Regulatory threshold (0.66–0.71). This is the most granular field — pinning a conclusion to a specific rule (a NAAQS limit, an ESA take threshold, a §106 adverse-effect finding). Many conclusions are not anchored to a single numeric threshold at all, and the distinctions are fine. It is reported descriptively as supporting context, never as a headline number.

The three scores that carry the findings — finding the determination, placing the resource, and getting the significance class — all clear or approach the standard bar.

How agencies stay below the line

Within FONSIs, the determinations sit — as they must — below the significance line: the agency either finds no significant impact outright or an impact that is less than significant, sometimes only with committed mitigation. Figure 3 breaks this down by resource area — each resource’s determinations split across the three outcomes, sorted so the resources most reliant on mitigation sit at the top, with the count and share behind each bar.

The dominant outcome is no significant impact, as expected for FONSIs. But the resources agencies analyze most — biological, water, cultural/historic, and public health — are also where the close calls concentrate: the magenta band (below-the-line only with mitigation) is widest for biological, soils/geology, and water. That is what makes the mitigated cases the real story.

Regulatory thresholds behind the calls

When a conclusion is anchored to a specific regulatory yardstick, which one? Figure 4 profiles the thresholds the FONSI conclusions cite — dominated by resource-specific numeric limits (other quantitative), wetland/floodplain extent, NHPA §106 adverse-effect findings for cultural resources, visual (VRM) classes, and the Endangered Species Act (take and jeopardy). This mirrors the resource pattern above: the same areas that drive mitigation are the ones with the hardest regulatory lines to clear.

Threshold identification is the extraction’s weakest field (see the validation above), so treat this profile as an indicative picture of which rules recur, not an exact census.

Mitigated FONSIs — the line itself

The most revealing determinations are the mitigated ones: impacts the agency says would be significant, brought below the line only by required measures. These show exactly where the line sits and what it costs to stay under it.

About 58% of these FONSIs are mitigated — at least one resource whose not-significant conclusion depends explicitly on committed mitigation. Which resources drive it:

Table 2: Resources ranked by how often their FONSI conclusions depend on committed mitigation.
Resource Determinations Mitigation-dependent Share
Biological 308 92 30%
Soils / geology 120 34 28%
Water 202 53 26%
Cultural / historic 194 42 22%
Public health 187 26 14%
Visual 126 14 11%
Air quality 132 14 11%
Noise 83 8 10%
Transportation 66 4 6%
Land use 142 5 4%
Socioeconomic 111 3 3%
Climate / GHG 64 0 0%
Share = fraction of a resource’s determinations that depend on committed mitigation (per-resource class signal, the high-precision measure).

The mitigation burden is concentrated in Biological (30%), Soils / geology (28%), Water (26%), Cultural / historic (22%) — the resources most often needing committed measures to keep a project below the significance line. That pattern is the deliverable’s core finding: biological, soils/geology, water, and cultural resources are where clean-energy projects most frequently sit at the line and are pulled under it by mitigation.

Reading volume and mitigation-intensity together sharpens the picture. Resources in the upper right are both analyzed often and mitigated often — the areas that most shape whether a clean-energy project can take the faster FONSI path.

What do these mitigations actually look like across the board? Two verbatim examples per resource, ordered from the most mitigation-heavy resources down — seasonal timing and species avoidance for biology, wetland minimization for water, cultural-resource protection measures, dust control for air, and so on:

Table 3: Representative mitigation measures behind less-than-significant-with-mitigation conclusions, by resource area.
Example mitigation drawn from the FONSI
Biological
Restricting construction to August/September is intended to mitigate potential nest failure and displacement effects on Red-throated Loons.
Potential impacts to desert kit fox would be avoided through compliance with general avoidance and mitigation measures identified in Appendix G.
Soils / geology
Use of BMPs and implementation of a construction SWPPP would ensure that short-term soil erosion and sediment transport impacts remain minor.
Soil erosion potential is limited by flat topography and controlled on-site via compliance with mitigation in Appendix B, resulting in a minor impact.
Water
Wetlands in the area were inventoried and potential impacts were mitigated in the design of the Proposed Action alternative.
Impacts to wetlands would be low, with only 0.01 acre of permanent wetland fill from structure replacement activities and impact minimization measures applied.
Cultural / historic
KSU committed to minimize or avoid potential effects to cultural resources via protection measures detailed in section 2.5 of the EA.
The PV array at Lakehurst may result in indirect visual effects to the LTA Historic District, but appropriate landscaping would minimize this effect.
Public health
With mitigation measures and BMPs, fire-prevention measures and traffic management would prevent disruption to fire, police, and medical emergency services.
With BMPs in place for portable toilet sanitary services during construction and operation, potential impacts from sanitary discharges would be non-significant.
Visual
KSU committed to minimize or avoid potential effects to visual resources through protection measures in section 2.5 of the EA.
VRM impacts are minor and localized, mitigated to the greatest degree feasible through Appendix B measures and project-specific stipulations.
Air quality
Air quality impacts would be low, temporary, and would not violate air quality standards, with dust control mitigation minimizing construction impacts.
Construction would cause unavoidable minor air quality impacts, but standard pollution control equipment on construction vehicles would mitigate these minor impacts.
Noise
Construction noise would be discernable up to 2,000 feet but would be low to moderate and mitigated by limiting activities to daytime hours where feasible.
Construction noise from initial vegetation removal would not significantly affect sensitive receptors or conflict with noise guidelines due to implementation of PCMs and the short duration of activities.
Transportation
Traffic delays from construction and lane closures would be temporary, with traffic controllers used where appropriate to reduce impacts.
KSU committed to minimize or avoid potential effects to transportation through the protection measures detailed in section 2.5 of the EA.
Land use
KSU committed to implement protection measures to minimize or avoid potential effects to land uses as detailed in section 2.5 of the EA.
Minor short- and long-term impacts to livestock grazing forage availability would not be significant with best management practices and mitigation measures.
Socioeconomic
Agricultural land disturbance would be temporary and mitigated by revegetation, scheduling around fallow periods, compensating landowners for crop loss, and maintaining fences/gates.
Verbatim from the model's per-resource rationale on mitigation-dependent (LTS-with-mitigation) determinations. Climate/GHG had no mitigation-dependent conclusions in the FONSI corpus.

Mitigated FONSIs are also broader analyses: a project that needs committed mitigation for any resource tends to address more resource areas overall — a median of roughly six versus four for non-mitigated FONSIs.

Read mitigation at the right grain. The document-level “is this a mitigated FONSI?” rate is robust. The resource-level attribution above uses the high-precision per-resource signal; a broader structured signal exists but over-attributes across resources, and its accuracy is ultimately bounded by upstream tagging (validation F1 ≈ 0.62). Treat the resource shares as a well-grounded floor, not an exact census.

EIS analysis

Note

Forthcoming. The EIS track is the above-the-line counterpart — which resources agencies judge significant, and where impacts are significant and unavoidable. It uses the identical extraction-and-validation machinery on the EIS corpus; the hand-labeled answer key is already built. This section will be populated once the EIS extraction pass runs. See Scope decisions below for the effort trade-off.

Scope decisions to confirm

A few items shape the deliverable’s scope and breadth. Each has a recommended default below; the goal is to confirm or adjust these before the full analysis runs.

  1. FONSIs only, or FONSIs and EISs? — the biggest decision. Significance calls appear in both document types: FONSIs capture the not-significant side (including the mitigated cases sitting right at the line), while EISs capture the significant side. The FONSI analysis is built and ready. Adding the EIS side means extracting findings from a ~6.1-million-page document set — a substantially larger AI and analyst effort that roughly multiplies the extraction cost and timeline and needs a retrieval-quality check first. Recommendation: deliver the validated FONSI analysis first; scope EISs as an add-on or a later phase once the FONSI work is in hand.

  2. Agencies: BLM + DOE, or broader? These are the only two agencies with complete coverage in the dataset and account for the large majority of clean-energy FONSIs; other agencies (NRC, Forest Service, BOEM) appear mainly on the EIS side, with partial coverage. Recommendation: BLM + DOE as the primary comparison; other agencies reported as context only, never mixed into the headline rates.

  3. What counts as a “resource area”? We read “across resource areas” as the standard NEPA environmental categories the documents are organized around — air quality; water (including wetlands and floodplains); biological resources; cultural / historic; visual; noise; soils / geology; socioeconomics (including environmental justice); transportation; land use; climate / greenhouse gases; and public health (including hazardous materials). Agencies judge significance separately for each, so this set defines the rows of the headline map. Confirm: is this the intended list, or does CATF have a specific set or a priority subset in mind?

Methods & required caveats

  • Agency scope — what the BLM + DOE limit costs. Of the 452 clean-energy FONSI projects in the corpus, 427 (94.5%) are BLM + DOE and carry the headline; 25 (5.5%) are dropped from the headline rates — 23 led by other federal agencies (which have only partial coverage in the dataset) and 2 flagged for manual scope review. They are held as a separate context universe, never mixed into the primary rates. So the BLM + DOE limit sets aside about 1 in 20 FONSIs; the far larger gap is the EIS side entirely (753 projects — the above-the-line story), which is a separate track not yet run.
  • D4 date/regime coverage. Many projects lack a high-confidence decision date; regime cells are confidence-gated and thin post-2023. EIS decision dates are frequently proxies.
  • EPA review letters (Clean Air Act §309) are out of scope. Under Section 309, the EPA independently reviews and rates other agencies’ environmental impact statements (e.g. “environmental concerns” or “objections”). Those comment letters are not in this dataset, so the report makes no claim about EPA’s own view of a project’s significance.
  • Clean-energy scope only (project_energy_type = 'Clean').
  • FONSI coverage for the mitigated/straight tiers derives from D6 artifacts.
  • EIS retrieval limits. The EIS tier is gated behind FONSI validation and a retrieval-recall spike; EIS findings are preliminary.
  • Validation sample size. Rare class/resource/threshold cells are reported descriptively, not as pass/fail macro-metrics.
  • Suppressed cells. Any cell below 5 is suppressed.
